Item text: the official English problem paper published by the International Mathematical Olympiad, imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/1992/1992_eng.pdf.
note: THE MAPPING NEEDS NO INFERENCE AT ALL: the live codes are problem1..problem6 and the official paper prints Problems 1 to 6. Each is marked out of 7 by the coordinators, which is the live 0-7 scale, and the six split three per day over two days -- carried in section_prompt. The persons are contestants. The alternative -- rendering every page and transcribing 60 problems by eye -- was considered and declined as disproportionate.

source_ref: Response data: Kaggle dataset 'imo-scores', CC0 1.0 Public Domain, confirmed on the source page. Item text: the official English paper, imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2016/2016_eng.pdf, transcribed from page images rendered at 150 dpi.
note: THE MAPPING NEEDS NO INFERENCE: problem1..problem6 are the paper's Problems 1 to 6, marked out of 7, three per day. 2016 IS THE ONE YEAR WHOSE NOTATION IS CORRECT, and for an awkward reason. Its PDF carries a symbol-font text layer that extracts as mojibake -- the header comes out as a run of dingbats where 'Monday, July 11, 2016' should be -- which is the same failure as the Kruti-Dev Hindi booklets in batch_203. Rather than ship garbage the pages were rendered at 150 dpi and read as images, so superscripts and subscripts survive here: P(n) = n^2 + n + 1 and A_1 A_2 ... A_k are written as such. The eight text-extracted years in this batch lose exactly that, so 2016 is better than its siblings rather than worse. The transcription is by hand and has not been checked symbol by symbol against the source.
public_note: The six problems of the 2016 International Mathematical Olympiad, each marked out of 7, three on each of two days. The statements were read from images of the official English paper because its PDF text layer is corrupted, which means the mathematical notation here is more faithful than in the other Olympiad years in this batch -- superscripts and subscripts are preserved.

source_ref: openpsychometrics.org/_rawdata/, archive 'AS+SC+AD+DO', CC BY 4.0. The archive ships codebook.txt beside data.csv; the codebook names the four IPIP scales with their ipip.ori.org keys, gives the response anchors verbatim, states that all items were prefixed with "I ", and lists all forty items against their codes. Codes assigned by data/ipip_openpsychometrics.r via select(starts_with(...)) with names kept.
note: ONE CODEBOOK SUPPLIES EVERYTHING AND THE SCRIPT RENAMES NOTHING, so there is no mapping step: the live code IS the codebook's code. TWO DELIBERATE DEVIATIONS FROM THE CODEBOOK'S LITERAL TEXT, both small and both disclosed here. (1) The codebook prints each item capitalised as a standalone list entry ('Feel comfortable around people.') while stating that all were prefixed with "I "; the administered sentence is therefore 'I feel comfortable around people.', so the first letter is lowercased when the prefix is applied. No other character is changed. (2) The codebook's anchor list contains a typo -- 'Neither agree not disagree' -- which ships corrected as 'Neither agree nor disagree'. THE SCALE STARTS AT 1 BECAUSE 0 MEANS UNANSWERED: the raw data codes a skipped item 0 and the processing script drops those with df[df$resp != 0, ], so all five labelled points 1-5 appear and nothing else does. This table is the Social Confidence scale (ipip.ori.org/newJPI-RKey.htm#Social-Confidence), ten items SC1-SC10, administered as part of an online DISC personality test alongside Assertiveness, Adventurousness and Dominance.
public_note: Ten items from the International Personality Item Pool's Social Confidence scale, answered from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Each item completes the stem 'I ...'. They were given as part of an online personality test alongside three other IPIP scales. A sixth response option meaning 'not answered' was recorded as 0 in the raw data and removed before this table was built.

source_ref: Steingroever, Fridberg, Horstmann, Kjome, Kumari, Lane et al. (2015), 'Data from 617 Healthy Participants Performing the Iowa Gambling Task: A Many Labs Collaboration', Journal of Open Psychology Data, doi:10.5334/jopd.ak, CC BY-SA 4.0; deposit osf.io/8t7rm (IGTdataSteingroever2014.zip, files choice_95.csv, choice_100.csv, choice_150.csv). Deck coding and payoff structure quoted from the paper. Item numbering reproduced by re-running data/iowa_gambling_task.R over those three files.
note: THE ITEM CODE IS A SCRIPT-GENERATED INTEGER OVER AN RBIND OF THREE FILES -- the hardest pattern SKILL.md names -- so it was re-run rather than reasoned about. The reproduction is exact: 65,291 long rows against the live table's 65,291, 339 items, and 617 participants as the paper reports. The three blocks are contiguous: items 1-93 are the 95-trial study, 94-191 the 100-trial study, 192-339 the 150-trial study. RE-RUNNING IT SURFACED A DEFECT IN HOW THE SOURCE IS READ, and the shipped text works around it. Each CSV has 95, 100 or 150 header names but ONE MORE FIELD per data row, because the subject-label column is unnamed. read_csv therefore slides the names one place left: the column it calls Choice_1 actually holds 'Subj_1', Choice_2 holds trial 1, Choice_3 holds trial 2, and the final field of every row -- the last trial -- has no name and is dropped. The script then renames Choice_1 to id, which is why the participant numbering comes out correctly at 1-617 and the shift is invisible there. It is visible only in the trial counts: the 95-, 100- and 150-trial studies contribute 93, 98 and 148 items, each losing its final trial to the shift and one more to drop_na. THE SHIPPED item_text USES THE TRUE TRIAL NUMBER (column number minus one), not the column number, so a reader is not misled by the off-by-one. Worth reporting upstream. resp IS THE DECK CHOSEN, NOT AN ACCURACY SCORE. The paper states '1, 2, 3, and 4 stand for deck A, B, C, and D, respectively'; A and B are disadvantageous (net -250 per ten cards) and C and D advantageous (+250), with frequent losses in A and C and infrequent in B and D. option_text carries those labels and correct_response is empty throughout, because a single draw has no right answer.
public_note: A card-choice task. On each trial the participant picked a card from one of four decks; two decks lose money in the long run and two gain. The item is one trial, and the response records WHICH DECK was chosen (1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C, 4 = D) rather than whether the choice was right -- there is no right answer to a single draw. Three versions of the task are pooled here, of 95, 100 and 150 trials, and the description of each item says which. TWO THINGS TO KNOW: the item numbers are not the trial numbers, because the processing script numbered items sequentially across the three pooled studies -- the trial number is given in the item description instead. And each study is missing its final trial, lost when the source files were read.
